findings.title: capabilityBundleVersion=2 is mutually exclusive with FLYWHEEL_CODEX_LEAD_SANDBOX, which every production launcher exports unconditionally
findings.detail: parseCodexLeadRuntimeConfig throws capability_bundle_legacy_sandbox_override when both FLYWHEEL_CODEX_CAPABILITY_BUNDLE_VERSION=2 and FLYWHEEL_CODEX_LEAD_SANDBOX are set; parseCodexLeadTuiRuntimeConfig (codex-lead-tui-runtime.ts:145) delegates to it, so the windowed production form is affected too. The registry-driven launcher scripts/flywheel-lead.sh:173 (compose_codex_child_env) unconditionally exports FLYWHEEL_CODEX_LEAD_SANDBOX=workspace-write and then execs codex-lead.sh, whose new canonical_lead_identity_resolve (scripts/lib/canonical-lead-identity.sh:178-181) exports FLYWHEEL_CODEX_CAPABILITY_BUNDLE_VERSION=2 for any lead with codexCapabilityBundleVersion:2. No launcher or sanitize_codex_child_env (flywheel-lead.sh:138-153) unsets it. I confirmed the throw by executing the built parser with exactly that env pair: 'THROW: capability_bundle_legacy_sandbox_override'. Failure scenario: set codexCapabilityBundleVersion:2 on the pilot Lead, launch normally -> the Lead exits at boot with an opaque error and never serves Discord. CI cannot see the contradiction because the runtime test helper fullEnv() (codex-lead-runtime.test.ts:52-72) never sets FLYWHEEL_CODEX_LEAD_SANDBOX while scripts/__tests__/flywheel-lead.test.sh:360 actively pins the launcher to keep exporting it.

findings.title: Managed CODEX_HOME config.toml permanently rejects the second and every later start of a v2 Lead
findings.detail: When <CODEX_HOME>/config.toml already exists, the code requires the previously recorded broker socket to still be under the CURRENT activationRoot (socketAllowed uses relative(activationRoot, socket)) and requires the rest of the old profile to deep-equal the new spec (line 116), allowing only brokerSocket and proxyPort to differ. Production rotates both roots on every process start: default-runtime.ts:144-145 mints activationRoot via mkdtempSync('/tmp/fw-cap-') and artifactRoot via mkdtempSync(projectRoot, '.flywheel-artifacts-'), while CODEX_HOME is stable per Lead and nothing in the v2 path deletes config.toml. I reproduced this against the built artifact with production-shaped inputs: start #1 OK; start #2 (rotate activationRoot+artifactRoot) FAILED capability_home_configuration_rejected; rotate activationRoot only FAILED; rotate artifactRoot only FAILED; rotate proxyPort only OK. ensureLeadCapabilityHome is on the live path (runtime-parent.ts:281), so startLeadCapabilityParent throws and the Lead is bricked until an operator manually deletes config.toml; launchd/cmux restart loops fail identically forever. The existing unit test passes only because capability-home.test.ts:22-40 reuses one stable activationRoot and a constant artifactRoot.

findings.title: Blanket (allow file-read*) is retracted only for $HOME and the enumerated credential roots, leaving /private/tmp, /private/var/folders, /etc and /Library readable from a --no-sandbox Chrome
findings.detail: The emitted policy is (deny default) -> ... -> '(allow file-read*)' (line 248) -> a deny over homedir() with carve-outs (line 253-256) -> readDenials over credentialPaths. Every deny is anchored at homedir() or a home-relative path, so /private/tmp, /private/var/folders/*/T, /etc, /Library, /opt and /Volumes stay readable. Since browser-config.ts:98 ships --chrome-arg=--no-sandbox (documented as Lead ruling ed48f532, with the outer Seatbelt named as the only boundary), a compromised renderer inherits that read surface plus process-exec of /bin/bash (line 243) and file-write* over qaRoot. Concretely it can read every other activation's control root under /private/tmp (default-runtime.ts:144 puts them there) and the founder's TMPDIR. Writes, network and $HOME remain closed, and I found no credential provably stored outside $HOME (the git askpass scripts at GitPushRunner.ts:342 and workflow-docs-git.ts:527 hold no secret), so this is defence-in-depth rather than a proven leak — but the in-code comment at line 245-247 ('Broad runtime reads retain explicit credential/project/probe denial') overstates what is actually retained.

findings.title: A rejected close() is memoized, so the daemon rebuild loop can never recover and the Lead silently stops serving
findings.detail: close() sets closed=true synchronously and caches `closing` on first call (lines 82-105). The async body can reject via capability_app_server_stop_unproved, sameDirectory(), or rmSync(root, {recursive:true}) at line 102 — which omits force:true, so a vanished /tmp root (tmp reaper, manual cleanup) throws ENOENT. In capability-tui-runtime.ts:110-118 the `await server.close()` inside the catch then rejects, so `server = undefined` on the next line never runs. Every later DaemonConnectionSupervisor retry calls server.assertCurrent(), which throws 'capability_app_server_closed' (capability-app-server.ts:126) — not the 'capability_app_server_exited' string the catch filters on — so it rethrows and the supervisor logs 'rebuild attempt failed (will retry)' forever at the backoff cap. The process stays alive so launchd never restarts it. Same missing force:true at line 54.

findings.title: With deliveryContext set, the idempotency key discards the caller nonce and includes only a hash of the text, so a second identical message is silently dropped but reported delivered
findings.detail: When req.deliveryContext is present the handler ignores the caller-supplied idempotencyKey/nonce and derives the key from sha256([projectName, leadId, deliveryContext, channelId, replyTo ?? null, sha256(text)]). deliveryContext is the journal entry id, stable for the whole turn, and nothing in the tuple distinguishes two separate sends. Failure scenario: a Lead issues two discord_send calls with the same text to the same channel in one turn (two 'done' acks, or the same status line twice) — the second hits the existing.status === 'sent' fast path at line 227, is never posted to Discord, yet returns httpStatus 200 with the FIRST message's id, so both the model and the receipt record it as delivered.

findings.title: A definitively rejected attachment send is reported as `unknown` and durably written as a maybe-delivered receipt
findings.detail: Any non-200 response is turned into `throw denied()` and caught into {status:'unknown'}. But the Bridge emits unambiguous rejections as non-200: 403 discord_scope_denied for a thread the Lead does not own, 503 provider_capacity when another Lead holds uploadActive (lead-capability-discord.ts:128-133), 401, and 400 invalid_upload. Failure scenario: Lead A calls attachments.send while Lead B's upload is in flight -> 503, nothing was posted -> parent returns `unknown` -> broker transitions the write receipt dispatched->unknown -> reconcile can never clear it, so the only way forward is minting a new requestId, i.e. exactly the blind-retry path the receipt machine exists to prevent. This is an outlier: handlers/bridge-discord.ts:157-206 and handlers/report-publish.ts:210-214 both decode the same 403 envelope into {status:'rejected'}.

findings.title: report.publish accepts 512 KiB artifacts but the Bridge body parser caps at 512 kb, creating a dead band that permanently burns the requestId
findings.detail: The handler accepts artifact.data up to 512 * 1024 bytes and then POSTs the HTML as a JSON string. The only body parser on that route is express.json({limit:'512kb'}) at bridge/plugin.ts:1810 (= 524288 bytes) and no larger per-route parser is mounted on /api/lead-capabilities/reports. JSON escaping plus the envelope makes the body strictly larger than the HTML, so anything near the cap — and quote-dense HTML well below it — gets a 413 before reaching the route. The handler maps that to {status:'unknown'}, the broker writes the receipt as unknown, and reconcile (line 256-262, /publish-receipt) never finds a report, so the same requestId stays unknown forever while the tool contract tells the Lead to reuse it.

findings.title: discord.thread.reply accepts 16 000 chars and silently posts up to 9 real messages while recording only the first id
findings.detail: discord.thread.reply uses the shared `text` schema (catalog.ts:47-50, .max(16000)) and the reply handler applies no length cap, unlike the sibling edit path which caps at 2000 (handlers/discord.ts:615). postDiscordMessageToChannel splits at MAX_DISCORD_MESSAGE_LENGTH=1900 and POSTs each chunk, but buildLeadDiscordSend keeps only messageIds[0] (leadDiscordSend.ts:50). Consequences: the providerRef and receipt understate what was posted (9 messages, 1 receipt); ownsSentMessage only records chunk 1, so editing or correcting chunks 2..N is permanently denied by the isEdit guard at discord.ts:634; and a failure on chunk k leaves chunks 1..k-1 in the channel while the receipt goes unknown, so any retry re-posts them. (The chunk-dropping in leadDiscordSend predates this change; what is new is exposing a 16 000-char write to the model through a receipt machine that assumes one message per operation.)

findings.title: The Lead model's entire network egress rides the browser's proxy under a 30 s per-socket idle timeout and a 64-connection cap
findings.detail: runtime-factory.ts returns proxyPort: browser.proxyPort, which permission-profile.ts:102 renders as the model's proxy_url with domains {'*':'allow'} — so the Codex Lead's own API traffic and the QA Chrome share one Node server with server.maxConnections = 64 (line 263), requestTimeout 30_000 (line 265), and socket.setTimeout(30_000, () => socket.destroy()) on every accepted connection (line 268) plus the same on the upstream socket. A reasoning request with more than 30 s before the first response byte is destroyed mid-request, and one content-heavy page can consume most of the 64-socket budget (Node destroys the excess with no response). Note the coupling direction: runtime-factory.ts:346-377 keeps the browser-owned proxy as the model's network path even when the browser itself fails to start, so a defect here takes down the Lead, not just the browser capability. I did not run this end to end.

findings.title: Chrome is spawned into its own process group by bundled Puppeteer, so process.kill(-pid) never reaches it and its profile is deleted underneath a live headed browser
findings.detail: BoundedStdioTransport spawns sandbox-exec detached and cleans up with process.kill(-pid, ...) — correct for the MCP node process, but chrome-devtools-mcp's bundled Puppeteer sets detached on its own spawn, making Chrome a separate process-group leader that the negative-pid kill cannot reach. close() also escalates to SIGKILL 250 ms after SIGTERM, skipping Puppeteer's own SIGTERM handler. browser-provider.ts:54 then rmSync(qaRoot, {recursive:true, force:true}) immediately after worker.close() returns, deleting the still-running browser's --user-data-dir and crashpad dir. Nothing verifies Chrome actually died; verifyNativeHeadedChrome is only called before close. Any hard death of the Bridge parent leaves a headed Chrome on the founder's screen with no owner.

findings.title: Attachment send caps per-file (25 MB) and count (10) but never the sum, so one request can force ~750 MB of transient Bridge RSS for a message Discord will always reject
findings.detail: MAX_ATTACHMENT_UPLOAD_BYTES = 250 MB + 64 KiB + 4 is the express raw() limit (lead-capability-discord.ts:151-155), and the per-file/per-count caps in attachment-upload.ts:24-34 and discord-attachments.ts:269,282 permit 10 x 25 MB. The Bridge buffers 250 MB in req.body, executeDiscordAttachmentSend copies each file (discord-attachments.ts:437), and sendDiscordAttachments copies again into Blobs (:292) — roughly 750 MB peak in the single Bridge process that serves the whole fleet. Discord's own per-message attachment budget is 25 MB, so the request is guaranteed to fail after the spike. uploadActive serializes but does not bound size.

findings.title: The capability broker unix socket carries no token; authentication is purely filesystem reachability, and chmod 0600 runs after listen()
findings.detail: accept() reads one JSON frame and dispatches into LeadCapabilityBroker.execute with no token, nonce or peer check — the only gate is the 0700 uid-checked parent directory (lines 35-42). Any process running as the same uid (including a Runner tmux session with full bash) can connect to /tmp/fw-cap-*/run-*/broker.sock and invoke every operation in that Lead's manifest: terminal.input, start_runner/send_runner, discord.thread.reply, linear.issue.*, github.pr.*. The Bridge HTTP legs by contrast require both the API token and the per-Lead carrierClaim. chmodSync(socketPath, 0o600) at line 57 runs after server.listen() at line 51, leaving a umask-dependent window. Honest caveat: a same-uid attacker can also read the Lead process env, so this is not uniquely weak — but it is the only surface in this change with zero credential. A per-activation random token compared with timingSafeEqual would close it.

findings.title: The re-check between the literal send-keys and the Enter send-keys can leave half-submitted text in a Runner pane
findings.detail: send() calls beforeSend() (the full guard: unchanged + observe + unchanged), writes the text literally, then calls beforeSend() again before pressing Enter. terminalCore() gives the whole call a 15 s deadline (assertCurrent), and the guard itself issues several tmux round trips each with a 5 s timeout, so under load the second beforeSend() can throw terminal_timeout or terminal_not_waiting AFTER the literal text is already typed into the pane. The Lead sees a failure and retries, appending the same text again, so the runner receives 'texttext' followed by Enter. The pre-change code sent text and Enter back to back with no intervening guard, so this partial-write window is new.

findings.title: Two new tests that spawn real subprocesses/servers use vitest's default 5 s timeout and fail intermittently under load
findings.detail: deployment.test.ts:111 spawns the compiled preflight CLI and git-push-transport.test.ts:107 stands up a real smart-HTTP server plus git subprocesses, neither with a per-test timeout override, so both inherit vitest's 5 000 ms default (packages/teamlead/vitest.config.ts sets no testTimeout). Running `vitest run src/lead-capabilities/__tests__` on a moderately loaded host, these 4 tests timed out at 5 s; re-running just those two files with --testTimeout=120000 they all passed in 16.5 s wall (24.8 s of test time for 10 tests). That is a flaky-red risk on any busy CI runner. An explicit timeout on the subprocess-spawning tests would fix it.

findings.title: codesign --verify --deep is given a fixed 60 s budget, below the observed host maximum, so the browser capability disappears intermittently and indistinguishably from a tampered binary
findings.detail: run('/usr/bin/codesign', ['--verify','--deep', pin.chrome.root], 60000) uses execFileSync with timeout, which SIGTERMs and throws. The same command on this host has been measured at 8 s–113 s depending on cache warmth and load. On a slow run verifyBrowserHostIdentity throws browser_host_identity_unverified, BrowserWorker.start throws browser_lost, and runtime-factory.ts:349 swaps in the browser_unavailable handler set for the whole activation. This fails closed, so it is not a security hole, but the Lead gets a silently and intermittently absent browser and browser_unavailable is indistinguishable from a genuine integrity failure. Same category: the fixed 5 000 ms whole-probe budget in browser-isolation.ts:99-102 must cover a cold sandbox-exec plus Node start plus two 1 500 ms TCP probes.

findings.title: migrateOperationReceipts / new OperationReceiptStore added to the constructor without the close-on-throw wrapper used by the sibling store
findings.detail: The receipts migration and OperationReceiptStore construction were added inside the SqliteJournalStore constructor with no try/catch, while the identical addition to SqliteOutboundDedupStore.ts:45-61 in this same change did get `try { ... } catch { this.db.close(); throw }`. If the migration throws, the better-sqlite3 handle plus its WAL/SHM files are never closed, and in capability-tui-runtime.ts the `journal` local is also never assigned so cleanup()'s journal?.close() is a no-op.

findings.title: The v2 MCP config pins enabledTools to ['lead_operation'], so the six advertised runner tool names are stripped
findings.detail: lead-capability-proxy.ts:164-175 additionally advertises RUNNER_ACTION_TOOL_NAMES as standalone tools, but the v2 lead_actions server config sets enabledTools: ['lead_operation'], so Codex filters them out. No capability is lost (runner operations remain reachable through lead_operation's oneOf), but the advertised tool inventory does not match what the model can actually call.

findings.title: The lead-operation CLI caps request input at 64 KiB while the client grants artifact.text.create a ~3.2 MiB frame
findings.detail: lead-operation-client.ts:10-16 gives artifact.text.create MAX_LEAD_OPERATION_FRAME_BYTES (6 * 512 KiB + 64 KiB) while the CLI's MAX_INPUT_BYTES is 65536, so any artifact.text.create larger than 64 KiB submitted through `flywheel-comm lead-operation` is rejected locally with request_input_too_large and never reaches the broker. Harmless if the CLI is not the intended path for that operation, but the two limits should agree or the CLI should say which operations it cannot carry.

advisories.detail: lead-operation-client.ts:10-16 gives artifact.text.create MAX_LEAD_OPERATION_FRAME_BYTES (6 * 512 KiB + 64 KiB) while the CLI's MAX_INPUT_BYTES is 65536, so any artifact.text.create larger than 64 KiB submitted through `flywheel-comm lead-operation` is rejected locally with request_input_too_large and never reaches the broker. Harmless if the CLI is not the intended path for that operation, but the two limits should agree or the CLI should say which operations it cannot carry.
